title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
lede: How fast, which way, and how quickly that's changing. The three ideas that describe every moving thing, from a jab to an 80,000-lb truck.

sections.md:
## Distance vs displacement
**Distance** is how much ground you covered. **Displacement** is how far you ended up from where you started, **and in which direction**.

Run one full lap of a 400 m track: distance = **400 m**, displacement = **0 m**. You ended where you began.

That difference sounds picky. It's the whole key to the next idea.

## Speed vs velocity
- **Speed** = distance ÷ time. It tells you *how fast*.
- **Velocity** = displacement ÷ time. It tells you *how fast* **and which way**.

Quantities with a direction are called **vectors** (velocity, displacement, force). Quantities without one are **scalars** (speed, distance, mass, time).

A truck going 60 mph north and one going 60 mph south have the **same speed** and **different velocities**. If they're heading toward each other, that difference matters a lot.

## Units and conversions
Science uses **meters per second** (m/s). Roads use miles per hour (mph). The bridge:

**1 mph ≈ 0.447 m/s** and **1 m/s ≈ 2.24 mph**

| mph | m/s | Feel |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1.3 | walking |
| 15 | 6.7 | sprinting human |
| 30 | 13.4 | city street |
| 60 | 26.8 | highway |
| 70 | 31.3 | interstate |

A useful image: at 60 mph you cover about **27 meters every second**, a little more than the length of a full tractor-trailer.

sections.title: Average speed
sections.problem: You drive 150 miles in 2.5 hours. What's your average speed?
steps: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
sections.answer: **60 mph**. Average speed tells you nothing about the moments you were stopped or going 75.

sections.md:
## Acceleration
**Acceleration** is how fast velocity **changes**:

**acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time**, written **a = Δv ÷ t** (Δ, "delta," means *change in*)

Units: (m/s) per second = **m/s²**.

A car going from 0 to 27 m/s (60 mph) in 9 seconds accelerates at 27 ÷ 9 = **3 m/s²**: it gains 3 m/s of speed every second.

Three ways to accelerate, because velocity has speed **and** direction:
1. **Speed up**
2. **Slow down** (negative acceleration, or deceleration)
3. **Turn**, even at constant speed. Your direction changes, so your velocity changes.

sections.q: A truck drives around a curve at a steady 45 mph. Is it accelerating?
options: Only if the road is banked
sections.why: Velocity includes direction. Turning changes the direction, so the truck **is** accelerating, toward the inside of the curve. That's why loose cargo slides outward.

sections.md:
## Gravity: the acceleration everyone shares
Near Earth's surface, anything falling freely (ignoring air) accelerates at **g ≈ 9.8 m/s²**, regardless of mass. A bowling ball and a baseball dropped together land together. Galileo figured this out around 1600; Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott proved it on the Moon in 1971 by dropping a hammer and a feather: with no air, they landed at the same time.

## Reading motion graphs
| Graph | Slope means | Area under it means |
|---|---|---|
| Position vs time | **velocity** | (not used) |
| Velocity vs time | **acceleration** | **displacement** |

A flat line on a position-time graph = standing still. A flat line on a velocity-time graph = constant velocity (zero acceleration). Steeper = faster change.

## The equations for constant acceleration
When acceleration stays constant, three equations connect everything (v₀ = starting velocity, v = final velocity, a = acceleration, t = time, d = displacement):

1. **v = v₀ + a·t**
2. **d = v₀·t + ½·a·t²**
3. **v² = v₀² + 2·a·d**

Pick the one that has the three things you know and the one you want.

sections.title: Why speed kills: braking distance
sections.problem: A truck at 25 m/s brakes at a steady 5 m/s². How far does it travel while stopping? What if it was going 50 m/s?
steps: Use v² = v₀² + 2·a·d with final v = 0 and a = −5 (slowing down).
sections.answer: **Double the speed, four times the braking distance.** Distance grows with speed **squared**. That's physics, not opinion, and it's why speed limits for trucks exist.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Average speed isn't the average of the speeds.** Drive 60 mi at 60 mph and 60 mi back at 40 mph: total time = 1 h + 1.5 h = 2.5 h, total distance 120 mi, average = **48 mph**, not 50. You spent more *time* at the slower speed.
- **Negative acceleration doesn't always mean slowing down.** It means acceleration points in the negative direction. If you're already moving in the negative direction, it speeds you up.
- **Heavier objects don't fall faster** (without air). Air resistance is what makes a feather drift.

practice.q: A runner covers 400 m in 80 s. Average speed in m/s?
Convert 70 mph to m/s (round to 1 decimal).

practice.why: Velocity has a direction. The others are just size.

practice.q: A car goes from 0 to 24 m/s in 8 s. Acceleration?
You run one full lap around a 400 m track in 100 s. Your average **velocity** is…
practice.why: Displacement is 0 (you ended where you started), so average velocity is 0. Average **speed** is 4 m/s.

practice.q: A rock falls from rest for 3 s. How fast is it going? (g = 9.8 m/s², ignore air)
On a **velocity-time** graph, the slope tells you…
practice.why: Slope of velocity vs time = change in velocity ÷ time = acceleration.

options: Driving a curve at a steady 40 mph
Cruising straight at a steady 65 mph
practice.why: Constant speed **and** constant direction = constant velocity = zero acceleration.

practice.q: You drive 120 miles to a delivery at 60 mph and back at 40 mph. What's your average speed for the round trip?
practice.why: Time out = 120 ÷ 60 = 2 h. Time back = 120 ÷ 40 = 3 h. Total: 240 mi ÷ 5 h = **48 mph**. You spent more time at the slow speed, so the average leans toward it.
practice.hint: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. Find each leg's time first.

practice.q: A truck's braking distance at 20 m/s is 40 m. Same brakes, same road, at 30 m/s. Braking distance?
practice.why: Braking distance grows with speed **squared**. Speed × 1.5 → distance × 1.5² = 2.25. 40 × 2.25 = **90 m**.
practice.hint: If speed goes up by 1.5×, distance goes up by 1.5 squared.

practice.q: A car brakes from 30 m/s to a stop in 75 m. What is the size of its deceleration?
practice.hint: Use v² = v₀² + 2·a·d with final velocity 0.

practice.q: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top, for an instant, its velocity is 0. What is its acceleration there?
options: It depends on how hard it was thrown
practice.why: Gravity never switches off. Velocity is momentarily 0, but it's still **changing** at 9.8 m/s² downward, which is why the ball starts falling. Zero velocity ≠ zero acceleration.
practice.hint: Is gravity still pulling at the top?
